utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I take it the appearances are as before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Well, no in the sense that it's a reduced appearance. It's simply myself, Joanna Korner, and Belinda Pidwell here today together with the case manager Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I say I do hope we're not going to be into this court too often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, is your witness here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he is, Your Honours. Can I just very quickly before I call him mention two matters -- three matters, in fact. The first is we're very sorry. We didn't appreciate until we spoke to the senior legal officer this morning that as you may have noticed when you were reading the report of Dr. Donia for Sarajevo, you never got the appendices. We -- it seems to be technical in that they were a separate document, and those appendices contain maps which is going to refer to this morning. The Defence all got them but for some reason they never got to you and you probably saw that, but we actually physically copied them, Your Honours now. If I can ask that the usher very kindly hand them up. The second matter is this: When Dr. Donia has concluded as far as we get in cross-examination tomorrow, can I raise with Your Honours the matter I raised last week, namely, that he's required as a witness in certainly one other trial as to how we deal with the question of other members of this office talking to him. And finally, Your Honours, tomorrow would it be suitable to deal with the question of the Defence application for certification to appeal Your Honours' order on Dr. Nielsen as a matter of an oral argument if you wish to hear from the prosecution at all? Our arguments are those we have enunciated in all the responses, but clearly he's going to be the first witness after the break on the 29th of September, so we need to have a ruling if not instanter, then certainly by the end of this week. And I'm being reminded of something. And the other thing is if you do require us to file it in writing then we'd have to do that today, but we thought it would be quicker to simply deal with this as an oral matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Will there be time to discuss this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, because Dr. Donia, as you will recall, needs to finish at quarter to 12.00 tomorrow, and we have the morning sitting. So we could deal with it -- I don't anticipate it will take very long for us to give any response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's bring up the matter tomorrow after his departure then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. In that case, Your Honours, without further ado, may I call Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Welcome to you, Dr. Donia, and welcome to everybody else in and around the courtroom, and thank you for coming. You are now going to testify as a Prosecution witness. I know that you have been here before, and so you have been through the exercise. You will start by giving your solemn declaration, and after that Mrs. Korner will examine you in chief for three hours, and then the Defence teams for the accused Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin will each be given some time to begin their cross-examination. The Chamber has ruled that part of your last expert report, the one on the siege of Sarajevo, will not be admitted fully, so you will only be examined-in-chief on three chapters of that report at this time, and then at a later stage you will be called back to -- to be cross-examined on -- on those three chapters. The order here is that we run -- the first session will last 85 minutes and then we need to take a break in order to change the tapes, and we will have a 20-minute break for that purpose. The second and third session today will each last 80 minutes. So that's the schedule -- plan for you, and I invite you to make your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Donia, could you give the Court your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Robert J. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think the Court has already been provided with a copy of your CV, so we needn't go through your qualifications and previous writings, but can we just briefly deal with some matters that are relevant to the evidence that you're going to give. First, I think it's right that you are the author of three books relating to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The most recent being entitled "Sarajevo, A Biography."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In addition to that, I think you have lectured extensively on the subject of Bosnia and Herzegovina generally and also on the conflict.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think we haven't actually added up the number of times but as Judge Harhoff has remarked, you have testified here before on at least a dozen or so occasions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've prepared a number of different reports for different cases, but for the purposes of this case can I just deal with the three reports that have been submitted. First of all, the report that was prepared for the case of Brdjanin and Talic, "Bosnian Krajina in the History of Bosnia and Herzegovina," which I think was prepared around 2002.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Secondly, the report prepared for the Krajisnik case, "The origins of Republika Srpska." That was also, in fact, prepared in 2002?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the most up-to-date is the report that you've done specifically for the purposes of the Karadzic case, which is due to start, entitled, "Bosnian Serb Leadership of the Siege of Sarajevo 1990-1995," and as you've heard from Judge Harhoff, only three of the chapters will be referred to.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just going to pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. We have a problem with the computer, so could I ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Defence, please. Microphone for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to interject for a moment, I'm taking it that we can discuss at the end of the evidence how the evidence will be admitted and exhibit numbering and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, turning straight away to the matters -- documents that you're going to deal with in evidence, is it right that you were asked by the Office of the Prosecutor to consider documents, perhaps the ones you considered most relevant for the purposes of this case given the time limitations on the oral evidence you are about to give?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you prepared a list which has been a bit altered because of various rulings. Can I start by asking you, first of all, about something of the structure and the ethnic structure of Bosnia in particular, and ask, first of all, that the map which was one of your Appendix 2 come up on the screen. Oh, I have to call -- I'm told I have to call the number, which is 3383. Apparently the one that's in Sanction, Your Honours, is slightly better quality for various technical reasons. So I don't know whether that would assist. I don't know. Your Honours, as I say, I'm told it's a bit clearer in Sanction. Yes, we'll swap it. That's it. Thank you. All right. Dr. Donia, can you tell us a little bit -- just explain, first of all, to us what that map demonstrates.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The map --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry, Dr. Donia, I gather there's another problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Well, the Bench can hear me but I'm sure interpretation cannot, so I don't know what you'd like to do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Court Reporter, can you hear if counsel speaks up? So speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll be loud and brief. One suggestion, on presentation of exhibits, the number my learned friend has mentioned, 3383 is the 65 ter number, which may ultimately get an exhibit number, and can I suggest that when the parties call up an exhibit using the 65 ter, they get marked for identification immediately so that we can coordinate 3383 with the exhibit number and not several days later or several pages later. The problem will be that this map is marked 3383. That is not the exhibit number. Ultimately, it will receive an exhibit number, but it will be very hard -- more difficult to track the connection between the number 3383 and the ultimate exhibit number, and I think it would be much more efficient if we mark it for identification with an exhibit number immediately. That's my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. In response to your observation I think if we give it an exhibit number right away, then there seems to be established automatically a link between that exhibit number and the 65 ter number, and that saves us from later having to come back to the document if we only do it by MFI. So I would prefer to the extent possible that exhibits are entered directly into the record with their proper exhibit number unless there is some -- something wrong, so to say, with the document that calls for a marking for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Apparently the microphone is working. Well, I quite agree and that was my suggestion is that this map has been -- is 3383 on the 65 ter list of the Prosecutor. I'm suggesting it be given an exhibit number at this point and marked for identification, and then when it's tendered and accepted then we -- there is no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make an even better -- maybe I hope -- sorry, a slightly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. -- I just need to consult with ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, I think I understand the gist of your suggestion, but I find it unnecessary. We will deal with this document. Dr. Donia will explain to us whatever it is he has to explain, and then as soon as we let the document go, we decide whether or not to admit it into evidence, and if it's admitted it's given a number. That saves us again from having to review all the MFI documents at a later point, which saves us time and energy. And so if I may add to this that I think your suggestion is also out of the normal way of doing things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make an [indiscernible] suggestion. Why not simply give the -- all the 65 ter numbers, they will remain as the exhibit numbers, and if they're not admitted then they won't appear. So this is Exhibit -- it will be Exhibit 33 -- whatever I said it was, 83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, no. This is impractical.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The way it works by experience is that when Dr. Donia has given us the information that you have asked him to give in relation to this document, then the Court will decide whether or not to admit it into evidence. Now, this is something which I don't see any reason why we should not, so we will give it an exhibit number right away and that will be Exhibit P1, I suppose. And if anyone wants to know what P1 is, then you can find it easily in the e-court system, and you can also track it back through the 65 ter number. That's the way we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Doctor. I'm so sorry. We hardly got started before we were stopped, but you were about to explain to us a little bit about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were about to explain to us what this map of the national composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina by municipality shows us.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The map before us shows Bosnia's -- I'll refer to it as Bosnia for short, if I may, 109 municipalities as of 1991. The municipality was the basic administrative unit of Bosnia's organisation. It was a concept that dated from the 19th Century, late Ottoman times, and the idea was that each municipality consisted of a central town which bore the same name as the municipality as a whole, surrounded by agricultural and forest lands and rural villages. The municipality was invested with considerable authority in the course of socialist years from 1945 until 1991 and, in fact, each had a Municipal Assembly by 1991, many of which were quite large. The map is, in my view, the best effort in two dimensions to capture the ethnic complexity of Bosnia, and even then only partially does so. It does so by portraying each municipality as consisting of one dominant group, whether that dominance is an absolute majority or a relative majority, and then presenting the members of other groups as bars in bar-chart form. As can be seen, there are certain areas of Bosnia, perhaps 8 or 10, 12 municipalities that have large, virtually overwhelming ethnic majorities of one group or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you can just perhaps -- before you move on can you just show us a couple of examples?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, well, the green area in the extreme upper left has two municipalities on the -- one is -- I can't even read them, the names, but they're right on the edge there which are almost exclusively Bosnian Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's Kladusa --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Velika Kladusa, and is it -- it wouldn't be Bihac. It's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the same goes for some blue areas along the lower left part of the triangle and some red areas -- I'm sorry, the blue areas being Croat, and the red areas also along the border, which are almost exclusively Serb and then much of the rest of the country being considerably more mixed. It was not uncommon for a municipality to have its central town have an ethnic composition different from the rural villages that surrounded it. So even this map in a sense consolidates and simplifies the ethnic complexity of Bosnia's landscape. And if I could just perhaps in a couple of sentences introduce the peoples or nations who are charted on this -- on this map. All three groups traced their origins to migration of Slavic-speaking peoples in the 4th to 8th Century's new era from the area of present day Poland and Belarus to south-eastern Europe. They developed into three different religious communities. The Slavic-speak Catholics became Croats, the Orthodox -- Serbian Orthodox becoming Serbs, and the third group converting to Islam became the Bosnian Muslims. And in the 19th century the intellectuals of the Serbs and Croats articulated a secular entity in addition to the religious foundations of their identity, and not until the 1960s did the Bosnian Muslims also articulate a secular identity, which made them then a third group with the Serbs and Croats who were recognised as constituent peoples in the constitution of 1974 that was in effect when the conflict began in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Doctor, what do you mean exactly by a secular identity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I mean is that they developed an ideology that the group in question was more than simply a religious community. It was distinguished by some combination of language, culture, and perhaps even religious traditions which gave it a distinct history, which gave it an identity that was something beyond purely membership in a faith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. And just for clarification, would that have any impact also on the language spoken, the sort of ethnic division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did in the sense that each group sought to codify a language from this sort of jumble of dialects and different manner of speaking of the South Slav tongues. They sought to codify a single language which they then designated as Serbian or Croatian or eventually in the case of the Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So just on that point, commonly certainly before the conflict the language is known as Serbo-Croat. Is that a proper --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, the languages are wholly mutually intelligible distinguished by only minor vocabulary differences, and prior to then -- I'd say the late 1980s were routinely called Serbo-Croatian and thought of as a single language.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, looking at that, would it be possible in your view, having looked at the background and the history of this, to divide Bosnia into ethnically separate geographic zones?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. The -- and many efforts were made to do that, and none of them was successful in actually delineating an area which was -- consisted purely of members of one of the three groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very briefly because we haven't got much time, did the three groups remain separate in terms of relationships, in other words, marriage?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: To some degree, but in the, say modern period, particularly the second half of the 20th century and particularly in urban areas, a great deal of intermarriage took place, and those people who entered into mixed marriages or the children of those marriages often sought refuge in some identity which was not one of the three groups. Most typically that identity was to call themselves Yugoslavs in the census category, and so on each of the censuses, the last two censuses, one finds a certain percentage of people identifying themselves as Yugoslavs, mostly in the cities and more in some cities than others, and that Yugoslav group was a very mixed category. It included some people, a lot of army officers, for example, who wanted to express loyalty only to the federal state of Yugoslavia, but it also included many people who rejected either a purely Serb, purely Croat, or purely Bosnian Muslim identity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I want to move, then, to the next document, please, which is a table of the -- oh, I'm sorry. It's 3384. 65 ter number 3384.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam, if you're finished with this, my question would be, do you wish to have it admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do. Can I say that I would be asking without having to do it each time for each of these documents be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You will not or you will?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I will -- I will each time if you want me to, but can we take it -- unless I say I don't want it admitted I would like it admitted. All right. No, I'll ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No. Mrs. Korner, there are two options: Either you ask for admission as we leave the document and move on to the next, or you bundle it up towards the end and then towards the end of the testimony you ask for this and that and the other document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's easier for the purposes of the transcript, as Mr. O'Sullivan points out, if I ask now that this may be admitted as an exhibit [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As an Exhibit, so it would be Exhibit 1, P1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So this is now admitted as P1, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move to the next document, 65 ter 3384, which is on the screen, which specifically deals, I think -- or perhaps you better explain what it shows, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. This table represents in figure form the graphic that we have just seen which was, of course, fine tuned to the level of municipalities showing that in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, about 17 per cent of the population identified themselves as Croats in the 1991 census, the 1st of April, 1991, about 44 per cent as Muslims, and about 31 per cent of Serbs, and the remaining 5.5 per cent as Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you've looked at the same -- or you have extracted information for the ten municipalities that make up Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Sarajevo represents a bit of an exception to the pattern of the municipality that I discussed earlier in that Sarajevo was actually made up of ten municipalities, giving this anomalous situation where a city actually consists of ten administrative units, which are called municipalities, and looking at those ten municipalities together, grouping them together, one can see that the population of Sarajevo was more Muslim than Bosnia as a whole, about the same percentage of Serbs, and much -- substantially fewer Croats, but that the percentage of Yugoslavs was higher. If I may, I've just noted an error in the percentage of Muslims in the B/C/S map, was not 3.5 per cent but it should be 43.5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Right. We're going to look at a map of Sarajevo at the end of these diagrammatic representations, but you then talk about Sarajevo's four peripheral municipalities. Could you just tell the Trial Chamber the names of those four.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Those four municipalities, Hadzici, Ilijas, Vogosca, and Trnovo were added to the city of Sarajevo in 1977. So they were the last to join the city, and they had a somewhat different composition than the rest of the city. As is shown here, a somewhat larger percentage of Serbs and a lesser percentage of Croats than the rest of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then let's move to the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be admitted as an exhibit in the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next document bears the number 65 ter 3385.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. This is a bad photo that reproduced even worse but simply captures the character of eastern Sarajevo and many other cities of Bosnia as high-rise buildings were built to house what were largely luxury apartments so that much of the urban population of Bosnia came to live in such structures, and of course, since they were all moving in, there was absolutely no ethnic distinction among the residents of these high-rises. So I wanted to show the picture just to indicate the, let's say, homogenising influence of urbanisation as it took place in Sarajevo and in other Bosnian towns, and of course other cities of the world as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the word you used was "luxury" was it, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That's what they were built as. Some of them didn't end up that way, but that was the intent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted, please, as P3.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then could we look, please, at 65 ter 3386.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, there is a question raised about whether or not these exhibits that we've seen, P1, 2, and 3, were actually included in your 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The report was. Your Honours, they were a part of the report. They were attached to the report. That's what I just explained. And Your Honours are admitting the report. Unfortunately by an error, I don't know why, when it was sent with the 94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't mind whether it stays as part of the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. I understand. But it's -- it's accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'm so sorry, Dr. Donia, that you had this interruption again. Can we look at this table now that you produced, as 3386 -- we produced -- and tell us -- explain what that shows.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This table shows the results of the November 1990 multi-party elections in the numbers of seats in the Bosnian Assembly, the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in the city Assembly of Sarajevo. What it shows is that the election results, in many respects, were census-like. They reflected the ethnic categories in the census in which three national parties emerged dominant: The SDA or Party of Democratic Action for the Muslims, the Serbian Democratic Party or the SDS for the Serbs, and the HDZ or Croatian Democratic Union for the Croats. In the case of the SDA and SDS, their percentage of seats in both the Bosnian Assembly and the Sarajevo City Assembly, is somewhat below their representation in the census in the population as a whole. In the case of the Croats, it's about the same. So there was -- it is not in a sense completely census-like. There is some -- some voters turned their back on their ethnic or national background in order to vote for Social Democrats and Reformists who represented non-national or even anti-national programmes. And again, the representation of those groups in the Sarajevo city Assembly is about twice what it was in the Bosnian Assembly, showing the greater propensity of the urban Sarajevo to drift away from these ethnic and national identities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just, as it were, as a side issue, the League of Communists also stood in the 1990 elections, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Social Democrats there is the name that I've given to the reformed League of Communists, which at a point actually had a name of League of Communists Social Democrats of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which I mercifully kept off the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now we're going to continue the theme of this inter-party split or party split, but just before we leave Sarajevo for the time being, can you look, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this is a separate map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you wish to have this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, yes. Could we have that exhibited, please, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we're going to show this in Sanction. We just thought Your Honours might like to see a proper map of Sarajevo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you, Dr. Donia, just first of all ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, it's in e-court, so he can draw apparently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can just put -- we can see -- maybe -- let's not. I don't want to spend too much time on this. Effectively I think the Court can see, the Trial Chamber can see, to the right Pale, just dealing with the municipalities that are part of our -- to the right Pale, then Ilijas is up there. Other way round, but never mind. And Vogosca in large letters. Dr. Donia, I've just got one question. Was there -- we can just about make out that there's major roads in the middle of the town, but was there any strategically important roads that were going to figure in the conflict to come?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The city of Sarajevo lying in an east-west valley, the entry and egress was very restricted to the east at the right of the map, and all went through essentially a narrow tunnel up in the direction of Pale. On the west end, the left side of the map, there were three major strategic passageways: The one that went through Vogosca we can see going to the north, the one heading out to the west going through Blazuj and Hadzici, which goes down to Mostar and the Adriatic coast, and then one which really doesn't connect very well with the city of Sarajevo to the south. The most passage -- the entry and egress of persons and goods from Sarajevo took place mostly along the three passageways to the east, west, and north, and therefore each went through a central town of one of the municipalities of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think unless Your Honours want anything else indicated on the map we'll move on from there, but may that map be admitted, please, as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please refer to the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will become Exhibit P5, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, I want, Dr. Donia, for a moment to -- you to deal with -- we looked at how the elections returned, married up with the ethnic distribution, as it were. Can we now look at a diagram.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has not been exhibited. It's simply a diagram to reflect evidence that -- it's easiest to look at it if it's -- it was attached to the pre-trial brief marked 6.1, which shows the make-up of the Presidency and government between January 1991 and March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How does that fit in with what was happening between the three parties?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The elections of 1990 resulted in victories for the three national parties, the SDS for the Serbs, the SDA for the Muslims, and the HDZ for the Croats. In negotiations prior to the calling of the elections, the Socialist era Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina designated two seats each on the Presidency to the three groups. That is, two were designated for Serbs, two were designated for Croats, and two were designated for Bosnian Muslims. In addition, a seventh seat was designated for the category of Yugoslavs. Because of the electoral arithmetic, the results ended up with three Bosnian Muslims. Being the most numerous group, they were able to triumph in the category of Yugoslavs as well. And then a seven-person Presidency with the president of the Presidency selected by the -- all members of the Presidency voting. However, in the period of the campaign, the three national parties were closely allied. They were all afraid of being swamped by the Social Democrats and Reformists and, therefore, cut a deal whereby the leading vote-getter of the three parties would designate informally who would be president of the Presidency. The next party, which turned out to be the SDS for the Serbs, would designate who would be the president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That turned out to be Momcilo Krajisnik. And the HDZ could designate who would be the president of the government position also known as prime minister or premier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So if we move the -- we've seen the Presidency. If we move the diagram up -- or down. Up, I think. What do we see there? How does that fit into what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the deputy prime ministers were also appointed as sort of a way to balance the ethnic structure at the top, and the -- if we could perhaps see the rest of the chart, the various ministers were also selected in accord with formulas that were agreed upon before the election in what's called the inter-party agreements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you. Now can I move to a slightly different topic. Did the leaders of the parties over the next period between the elections, 1990 and what happened in 1992, express publicly any view that they had about the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's start with Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Okay. The debate about the constitutional future of Bosnia raged during the campaign was the only issue on which the three parties, three national parties, had sharp disagreements at that time, but one of those parties, the Muslim SDA, was headed by Alija Izetbegovic, who had quite a political history and, therefore, became both a unifying figure amongst Bosnian Muslims but a polarising figure amongst non-Muslims, particularly Serbs. He had been imprisoned on two occasions in the late 1940s and then again in 1983 for being a political dissident, was prosecuted by the Socialist regime, and in the late 1960s had written a book called the "Islamic Declaration," which became the central focus of the criticism of him, particularly by those people, the Serbs and Croat nationalists who wanted to identify him with a project of creating an Islamic state in Bosnia. And I think it's worth looking at Izetbegovic's "Islamic Declaration" just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's about to -- I'm sorry, now I have to call you up, don't I? Could I have 65 ter 3388?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Islamic Declaration was written in the late 1960s in the aftermath of the Arab-Israeli war of 1967 which, of course, was won decisively by Israel and set off a great deal of soul searching amongst Muslim and Islamic -- Muslim intellectuals and Islamic figures globally. The Izetbegovic "Islamic Declaration" was written to contribute to that debate. As a book, it never mentioned Bosnia-Herzegovina, never mentioned Sarajevo, never mentioned Yugoslavia. It was a pure contribution to the global discussion of Islam, and Izetbegovic called for a renewal, Islamic renewal, while rejecting the two -- what he saw as extreme paths of radical secularisation and the extremely conservative mullahs and hodjas of the Islamic faith.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we pull up page 10 of this, Y 0164151.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 51 -- okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- passage -- okay. In this passage, Izetbegovic levelled his criticism at the Islamic religious establishment, writing: "Theologians have turned out to be the wrong people in the wrong place." Now, when the Muslim world is giving all signs of an awakening, this class has become an expression of all that is gloomy and sclerotic in the world. He was equally critical of modernising secularists, but levelled this criticism of the clerics as well. And ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look at --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: One more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'll just get the page number out. Page Y0164205, and 6.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. He was also critical of nationalism in the Islamic world, writing on this page at the bottom of the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not sure I -- just -- just pause for a moment. I don't think it's come up yet. This thing takes a long time, obviously, to change.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think it's a few pages beyond what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can we go on, please, sorry, to Y0 -- 205? Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The central paragraph of this page, the last sentence: "Pan-Islamism has always sprung from the very heart of the Muslim people, while nationalism has always been imported goods." This is perhaps the only sentence in the entire tract which could be considered a possible reference to something that was going on then, because it was in the 1960s that the Bosnian Muslims were articulating a secular identity, as I had indicated earlier, a secular national identity. And clearly he was on the other side of that issue. He did not favour a national identity or nationalism for Muslims. He continued on the next page --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's pause for a moment while we get that up. So that's 206. Yep.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The sixth line of the first paragraph: "The creation of the European Economic Community, although this claim may seem unacceptable at first sight, is the most constructive event in 20th-century European history. This super-national structure is the first real victory of the European peoples over nationalism." Again making clear his feelings about nationalism.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Now, this book does contain some statements about what Muslims should do, how they should form a state or society at the point that they have a majority, and these seem to be cautions against jumping the gun in a sense, for Muslims to create institutions separately or prior to the time that they hold a majority, but it is those quotes which became the central focus of critics of Izetbegovic who charged him with wanting to create an Islamic state in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that was -- are there any other passages which you think would be useful for the Court to look at? I think not. No?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think we've seen --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So there's -- that's the, as it were, the outlook expressed by Alija Izetbegovic. What about the Serb side of the line, as it were? Were any views expressed --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, yes. Could that be admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, may I remind you that according to the procedural guidelines that we have issued, you have to be specific about which parts of larger documents, such as books, you need -- or you wish to have admitted into evidence. So if we're speaking about only these two pages, it's not a problem, but I hope that this is what you had in mind and not the entire book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. For the moment we'll stick to the pages -- I think it's three pages, in fact, that we've referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And can you, for the purpose of the Registrar, just identify those three pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will become Exhibit P6, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we look at, as it were, some of the thinkers on the Serb side. Can you tell us something about a gentleman named Jovan Raskovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The Serb viewpoints on Bosnia's future emphasised the national factor. They became very critical of the Bosnian Muslims for being less than avid nationalists and for favouring a civic option. At the same time, they denounced the Muslims for being fundamentalist and wanting to establish an Islamic state. Several of them, in their more candid moments, dismissed the notion of fundamentalism in Bosnia. Radovan Karadzic did so actually in, I think, his first or second press interview in the course of the campaign in 1990, and so did Jovan Raskovic, who was the founder of the SDS, the Serb National Democratic Party in Croatia, who also was an important figure in founding the Serbian Democratic Party in Bosnia. Raskovic actually died in July 1992, a couple months after he stated these words, but it was his view --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll call up the document.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up please 65 ter 3390. Thank you. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is, I think, an interview, is that right, with Mr. Raskovic --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- in a publication called "Borba."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. And in that interview on -- it's the third page, which is, if I can cite the ERN, 03015931, which is, I believe, up now, stated the view that -- in this response to the question about Karadzic: "First, I never had the impression that the SDA, regardless of the fact that it was Islamophile, was a danger for the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But, what is done is done. It is different with the Croatian authorities and the Serbs in Croatia." And skipping the next line: "Conspiratorial policy was necessary in Croatia because it could not be any different. Such a policy was not necessary in Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So at that stage, certainly, and this is April of 1992, is it not, I think --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: 22 April 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So even at that stage Mr. Raskovic was saying that in his view there wasn't a malicious intent against the Serbs by the --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That was his view --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- for the situation in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then I think around or -- the time of the elections, Izetbegovic expressed what he wanted or what he saw for -- for Bosnia. Is that right? If we look, please, at 3 -- 65 ter number 3391.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Did I ask for that last article to be admitted? I did. Could that be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P7, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is -- is it a publication called -- I think you better say it, not me, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. "Nedeljni Glas," which simply means "Weekly Voice," the weekly magazine of a daily newspaper in Banja Luka, which was named "Glas" or "Voice."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was this an interview -- sorry, I'm just checking this is the right document. I thought -- no. Just for one moment. Yes. Was this Izetbegovic speaking, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is, yes, a paraphrase of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of what he said.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- of Mr. Izetbegovic's position in this article by a journalist, and accurately reflects the position of the SDA at that time in the -- in the constitutional question of Bosnia's future. There was a dispute about Bosnia's future, let's say at a philosophical or ideological level, but there was also a dispute about its future as a discussion of political options or constitutional solutions, if you will. And the second full paragraph on this page which begins "That is the real thing," expresses this position: "Bosnia-Herzegovina wants a contemporary state. It is not favouring the confederate concept," or a confederation, in other words, "as suggested by Slovenia and Croatia, nor is it in favour of the hard federal concepts as proposed by the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Bosnia-Herzegovina wants the middle, it wants a formula that would reconcile these two suggestions and therefore is for a new agreement, for a charter on the Yugoslav state community." Now, this places Izetbegovic and the Bosnian Muslims in the middle of the ongoing debate among presidents of the six republics of Yugoslavia. On the one hand, Milosevic and Bulatovic for Serbia and Montenegro wanted a firm, federal state. They wanted a state that was at least as strong as it was then, and if they could, they wanted to strengthen the federal state. Serbia -- or Croatia and Slovenia, on the other hand, who were moving increasingly towards independence, wanted a confederation in which sovereignty would reside in the individual republics as much as in the federal state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: And the two republics that were sort of caught in the middle between these viewpoints were Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia and their respective presidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at almost about exactly the same time, November of 1990, as what Karadzic said on this topic, can we call --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this -- the last document, 3391, please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P8, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then can we call up, please, 3392.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, I think this is an article in "Glas"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This, yes. It is an article in the Banja Luka newspaper "Glas" taken from the Yugoslav news agency, which was known as Tanjug, which originated a lot of the stories that appeared in local newspapers throughout Yugoslavia, and in it Karadzic is paraphrased as expressing the viewpoint here of Serbs, saying: "The Serbian people cannot accept an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina which exists alone or in a confederation with other states," so he rejects the confederate -- confederate option, "or any other form of state organisation that would separate them from the Serbian people as a whole or would turn them into an ethnic minority. Then on the very last page of this document he express -- he again --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, let's go to --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- paraphrased --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't -- you've got the last page up. Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- as saying: "He repeated the standpoints according to which Bosnia-Herzegovina within a confederation could not be brought about without a civil war." Is again something that he stated a number of times and reported here by Tanjug which is -- could be considered, I think, a very, say, fair-minded reporting agency at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could that please be admitted as an exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P9, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, that was in -- in 1990. When we get into 1991, how was this discussion or argument about federation or confederation being perceived by the -- in particular, the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb position on this hardened. It didn't really harden. It was firm and remained firm in the time after the election. It was to them a non-negotiable position that if Bosnia were to be a state in which Bosnian Serbs wanted to live, it had to be a part of a federal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, let's look next, please, at document 14 -- 65 ter 1493, which is the 4th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 21st of December, 1991, and I want to look, please, at a speech made by Mr. Buha.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. At this -- at this time, the debate about Bosnia's future constitutional status, was really the sharpest public controversy at the time, and Professor Aleksa Buha, who later became the Foreign Minister of the Republika Srpska, expressed, I thought quite graphically, this difference between the Serb or Bosnian Serb viewpoint and the viewpoint that he considered the other groups, mainly the Muslims but also the Croats, to be espousing at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we need to look, please, at page 00939642. I think we --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't see the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you not see it? If we look "All this national identity."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Middle of the page, the first -- let's see here. It's now, as I look at it, the third paragraph on the page beginning: "All this, that is, national identity, national equality, nation as a fundamental unit of individual and collective life that was once sacred to them," that is the Croat and Bosnian Muslims --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but the Serbian page does not correspond, so the clients cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It should be 00898134. The -- the accused will presumably hear the translation through their headphones in any event. I'm sorry, what? SA02-5071.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the matter of accuracy, they should be able to see the document, the original of the document, not the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. We're bringing it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the B/C/S it's the middle paragraph on the page as it stands now, and may I commence again with the English?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: "All this, that is, national identity, national equality, nation as the fundamental unit of individual and collective life, that was once sacred to them, our partners," again referring to the SDA and the HDZ, "have forgotten overnight and adopted the civil principle and started advocating civil society instead of national society. Presumably this principle would have deemed -- been deem an anathema at the Yugoslav level, but now it is considered a perfect solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina." It's actually in the middle of a quite learned discussion of the origins of the civil concept and national society which he put forth, but emphasising, kind of encapsulating this Serb view that the Muslims were advocating a civil state, that is, equality of all citizens, in expectation that they would have a majority some day soon and therefore take over the state. That's the essence of the Serb viewpoint on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He then goes on, does he, to talk about the ethnic composition of BiH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can that, Your Honours, please be made an exhibit, and could we have the whole document exhibited, because it's going to be referred to by other witnesses as well, so it would make sense to have it as an exhibit already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How long is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How many pages? I can't tell you. It's probably -- it's one of the Assembly sessions. Fifty pages. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P10, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we now move on before the break, finally, to consider the question of regionalisation. Was that something that was figuring in SDS thinking at this stage?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The SDS, anticipating a move toward sovereignty or independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, began organising areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina which had substantial Serb populations, with the idea of combining Serb majority municipalities and forming regional associations for the purpose of rejecting some of the functions and sovereignty of the Bosnian state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you dealt with that in your report, and we needn't bring that up, but you did for the purposes of the Brdjanin case, but can we have a look, please, at a speech made by Krajisnik, please, in 1991, 65 ter 1484. Which was the 2nd Assembly of the Bosnian -- 2nd Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 21st of November. And could we have on that page 00930300 in English, SA01-2009 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. In this couple of sentences, Krajisnik expresses the purpose for which regional associations were being formed. The first one, the most important one, of course, being the community of municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina. And using -- looking at the first full paragraph there, actually the sixth line on the page: "It is our goal to decentralise all republican funds, to keep most of the income of citizens and legal entities in their municipalities, regions and autonomous districts, so that only limited contributions are paid to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "We have a duty to determine the function of regions and autonomous districts with a view to preserving the unity of the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So what's happening here? This was a -- or you should tell us, but regionalisation was being used to do what in political terms?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: To become autonomous from Bosnia-Herzegovina and achieve basically local control of tax monies and key decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that's 85 minutes. Oh, yes, and please may I tender again the whole document. It's the Assembly minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: These are the minutes from the second Session in November --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] The 2nd Assembly, yes, and I'm sure [overlapping speakers] -- they're going to be referred to over and over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit P11, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And we will adjourn and reconvene at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could -- could I -- could we go back to Exhibit P9, please, last -- last page. I think there's something wrong there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P9. Is that the last exhibit that Dr. Donia looked at before this one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, no. No, no, it's P9. We're at P11, I think, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Was the paraphrasing of Karadzic's views.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The paraphrasing of Karadzic. Ah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Last page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Karadzic. That's 3392, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Last sentence. Shouldn't we read "Could not be brought without a civil law"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: A civil war -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. Just for information to the parties and to the two accused, I would like to refer to a conversation that I had with the Prosecution just here on the break about the seeking admission of some of the documents which we have just recently admitted into evidence, and the problem that I raised with Mrs. Korner was that it appeared that some of the documents that we did admit did not appear on the 65 ter list, and I would like to repeat that the rule for the future is that if a document will be sought admitted into evidence through a witness, then that has to be notified to the Defence, first of all, in advance and then also to the Chamber, because otherwise we will be unable to familiarise ourselves with the documentation prior to the testimony of the witness. And that goes also for expert witnesses such as Dr. Donia. The ruling I passed down yesterday, or the Chamber passed down yesterday, concerned, first of all, the documents that were in the Sarajevo report -- or the three chapters that we have admitted from the Sarajevo report. The same ruling -- that ruling does not -- or did not apply to the previous reports, because we thought that the previous reports had already been dealt with and that you were -- that you had made up your mind in advance as to which documents from those earlier reports you would put to Dr. Donia and thus have admitted into evidence. Now, we will just leave things as they are at the moment because the Defence did not object, and so the documents that you have admitted will stay admitted, but for the future, I would like to ask the Prosecution and the Defence when it becomes their turn to make sure that the other party and the Chamber is duly notified of each and every document that you wish to have admitted through a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Right. Very quickly because I don't want to waste time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Exactly, so I think we should just leave it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I -- then come back and deal with that point later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Just a correction to the transcript. When Honourable Judge Delvoie intervened, it was on the page 33, line 20, in transcript said civil law instead of civil war. Just correction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one suggestion that may remove such difficulties in the future. I suggest that admission of evidence be sought after the testimony of a witness to avoid situations wherein the Defence is unable to check whether a certain document is on the said 65 ter list or not. Therefore, I suggest that the decision to admit a certain piece of evidence be taken after the testimony of a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we get -- could we -- could I get on with the witness and we can discuss this later? I don't think that's helpful, and the point I'm going to make is that all these documents I've been referring to by 65 ter number are on the application we made to add, which was dealt with on -- which was filed -- I can't remember the date, but I think it was on -- on the 14th of September, and we took Your Honours' ruling to exclude certain things to mean that the others were allowed in. All the documents were listed on one -- one motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We'll deal with that when we're over with Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So let's proceed for now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I'm sorry again about that. I'm afraid at the beginning of a trial things go awry. Can I just ask you to look there, please, at one further document on the subject of regionalisation, and can I ask that what I'm calling 65 ter 3395 be put up on the screen. Which again is another "Glas" article. And the number -- yes. Could we turn to the next -- well, first of all, I think the article itself is headed "Hasty Regionalisation," and then can we turn, please, to the other side of the translation with the number L0099855. And this, I think is an interview -- or it's a summary, is it not, of what Mr. Dodik said?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just tell the Court, because I don't think I've explained about Dodik yet, who Dodik was -- is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to the manner this question is asked. This is an article. Therefore, it is hearsay evidence. The article mentions the name "Dodik," but that does not necessarily mean that the article reflects faithfully what Dodik had said. This is double hearsay evidence. The witness has told us about the role of the media. This witness is not an expert in media issues. At least he was not represented that way by the Prosecution. I object to this whole line of questioning and the presentation of news articles. Transcripts of Assembly sessions are another matter. What probative value does the conclusion of Mr. Donia have based on reading newspaper articles about which we know nothing? Maybe they do not reflect faithfully what the original speakers had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: One more thing, Your Honours. In light of your ruling just at the beginning of this, this document, 3395, is not on the 65 ter list either. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for making this note, Mr. Zecevic. Now, as for the objection raised by Counsel Krgovic, we will overrule your objection because, first of all, hearsay evidence is, as you know, admissible before this Tribunal, and secondly, and more importantly, the evidence that goes in is not the article with the presentations of what Mr. Dodik may have said but what Dr. Donia's comments to the article is going to be. So that is what we will have a look at when we consider the evidence in the end. So we will attach weight to Dr. Donia's opinion about this point of view and not to the article as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, before you were interrupted, you were just telling the Trial Chamber who Milorad Dodik was -- is.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milorad Dodik --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I raised the issue that it wasn't on the 65 ter list. I believe the Chamber should rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zecevic. I thought that I had made clear in my comments just a while ago that there seems to be some degree of uncertainty as to exactly which documents had been notified in the last motions made by the Prosecution and that we would deal with it at the end of Dr. Donia's testimony or after Dr. Donia's testimony so as to avoid losing time at this moment for discussion -- for discussion of administrative matters. Let's -- let's deal with these issues when Dr. Donia is through and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I -- with all due respect, I think it should be dealt first with the documents which are not on the 65 ter list before we hear the witness reflect on these documents. That is my opinion. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I agree that this is the principle, but as I have told you, the Prosecution is of the view that they have notified us, and there seems to be a misunderstanding about the contents of the ruling that we handed down yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think in light of that uncertainty I think the best thing we can do now is move on and then settle the issues later on. Is that okay, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have to accept the ruling of the Trial Chamber. There is nothing else. I hope we will resolve the matter afterwards. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Mr. Zecevic's case manager calls up the motion that was served, you'll see that all these numbers are on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again I apologise, Dr. Donia. Maybe this time you'll be allowed to tell the Court who Mr. Dodik is.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: If Mr. Dodik can get a word in. He is currently the president of Republika Srpska and has been in that position for several years. In 1991, he was elected as a Reformist --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I really object to this now. This is the third time that Dr. Donia has been interrupted. Unless this is of extreme importance, may I ask that Mr. Pantelic waits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, could we hear what his objection is?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To help Dr. Donia. Maybe you may state corrected Mr. Dodik is not the president of -- he's the prime minister. Just a matter of -- thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. May I suggest that issues of this character be raised by you during your cross-examination so as to avoid numerous interruptions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In any case, thank you for the correction. He is the prime minister of Republika Srpska. In 1990 he was elected to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the municipality of Laktasi on the Reformist ticket and as such was a Serb in a party that had no -- no national allegiance. It was a non-national party. When the -- several municipal assemblies in the region of north-western Bosnia announced that they were joining the community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina, it set off a controversy amongst all party leaders in that area. The SDS leaders had presented this motion -- or movement for the creation of a municipal association as simply following on a Socialist era practice of associating municipalities for certain limited functions. Things like a water district or schools or a particular municipal kind of project. And other party leaders took issue with the notion that this was simply an apolitical or a national project, and Dodik was one of those who was quoted as such at this time, saying: "This means that we as parties," meaning political parties, "were not engaged in all this. I personally consider it politically highly illiterate and impudent that certain municipal assemblies voted on the initiative in spite of the fact that none of the deputies received any materials, that the explanations were distributed verbally, and that the vote on such important decisions was held directly there and then. It is, therefore, our stance that the initiative of the Bosnia-Herzegovina republic authorities must by all means be supported and that this problem has to be approached more seriously and studiously and that it must be accompanied by a simultaneous public debate especially since the initiative originated from one party only, the SDS."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. All right. That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I ask that that document be admitted. Now, I don't know how you're going to deal with it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P12, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, we object to admission of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much. Dr. Donia, I want to move now to what happened at the Assembly meeting, the Bosnian Assembly meeting in October of 1991, the 14th of October. What in your view emerged from the -- the meetings that occurred that day that we're going to look at, and we'll start, first of all, with 65 ter number 2296.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The date of 14, 15 October 1991, I think is a -- it's a pivotal day filled with events that -- in which these contrasting political philosophies and constitutional positions collided, and they collided in the context of the 8th Session of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which began a multi-day session the week before to debate the constitutional future of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The SDA, the Muslim party, and the HDZ together arrived at that session with two proposals: One which has become known as a declaration of sovereignty, ascribing sovereignty to Bosnia-Herzegovina or, more specifically, citing an existing constitutional amendment which provided that Bosnia and Herzegovina was sovereign, and the other was a platform directed at the Presidency to guide its negotiations in the context being -- then held by the European Union -- European Community. So on that day three important things happened: Number one, the debate became very heated, and Radovan Karadzic uttered some words that he had previously only expressed in private telephone conversations, which threatened the future existence of the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause for a moment. We'll just -- the Trial Chamber saw, in fact, the video of that speech yesterday, but just -- can we have page 3 in English and in B/C/S just so that we can see.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Okay. If I may -- just these couple of selected passages. About halfway down the page, the sentence that begins: "We shall disable you to carry out violence against Serbian people, constitutional violence, in front of local and international public, because after the constitutional violence, all other violence will come. We won't be consulted regarding this situation anymore." Then skipping one sentence: "Knowing that in Bosnia-Herzegovina that hell would be 1.000 times worse, and there would be no way to stop it." Again, I see an error in the English here. And then the last two sentences on the page: "It is not good what you are doing. This is the road that you want Bosnia and Herzegovina to take, the same highway of hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia went through."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as I say, I think we can leave it there, Dr. Donia --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- because the Trial Chamber heard it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask the admission of the minutes of the Bosnian Assembly for the 14th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It is admitted. And may I suggest that in view of the objections made by Counsel Krgovic that we MFI P8, P9, and P12, if that is possible, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours. 65 ter 2296 will become Exhibit P13, and Exhibit P8, P9, and P12 are now marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just tell Your Honour that this one's been on our 65 ter list all along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But that's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P13.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just -- I just need to raise the attention of the Trial Chamber that the Serbian version of the document does not correspond to the English, the page. So in order to avoid future problems with that, I would like to -- because the Serbian text is cut halfway through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] yes. We'll try and make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, please be careful and make sure that where pages turn over that the defendants are notified.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I -- I apologise to Mr. Zecevic. I agree it's difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, that's the Assembly. That evening was there a party council meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. If I can just describe the background to that party council meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Following Dr. Karadzic's speech, the president of the Assembly, who was an SDS leader, Mr. Krajisnik, adjourned the session, and while many Serbs were still in the hall, the vice-president of the Assembly reconvened the session, and that reconvened session was attended only by members of the HDZ and the SDA, the Muslim and Croat parties, and in that reconvened session they then passed the two documents that I referred to, the memorandum of sovereignty and the Presidency -- or the platform, and that led the members of the SDS, Karadzic and others, to claim that this was illegal and unconstitutional, and they immediately convened or later that -- this was 3.00 or 4.00 in the morning, and they convened for that evening a session of the SDS party council. The party council was a body that included not just the day-to-day party leaders but also a number of professors and other intellectuals who were not actively day by day engaged in the party but were frequently acting as advisors, and at that party council meeting they discussed future steps to take in light of the decision of the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please, on the screen 65 ter 3398, at page -- the one page. The first page. And hopefully the B/C/S is the same. Page 2 on the B/C/S I'm told.

utterances.speaker: MR. HICKS
utterances.text: Terribly sorry to interrupt, Your Honours. Could we request that the Registrar also or the Court Officer also enlarge the B/C/S portions as they do for the English. They're having trouble reading the exhibits on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hicks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, we see there the minutes, 15th of October, and underlined on that page is something said by Mr. Todor Dutina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tell -- please be kind enough to tell the Trial Chamber who he was.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I -- I can only identify him as a member of the party, SDS party. And the -- this was in a sense a wide-ranging discussion of which we have only minutes, not transcript. So this is a secretary's rendition of the main points that were made rather than a verbatim transcript, but he is quoted as saying what some -- a number of other members of the council also stated: "Tonight we must put an end to the illusion that it is possible to find some kind of joint existence with the Muslims and Croats ..." There were also a number other people who expressed the idea that they should give the Muslims and Croats, that is the HDZ and the SDA, one last chance to -- to rescind their decision of earlier that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, may that be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P14, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally, can we look at one last party council meeting, which should be 3398. On this date. Oh, is it? I thought there was three. All right. I'm sorry, you're quite right. I got myself mixed up there. All right. So that was October -- or, rather, before I move on, Dr. Donia, are there any other meetings that took place at that -- around that period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There is just one other statement in that party council meeting --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ah, right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- that I think is -- remarkably it was prescient in the sense that Mr. Miskin, misspelled Niskin here, it's the third page of this document, outlined steps that he proposed the SDS should take.
